To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

- stacking several layers of unsupervised learning is a good way of extracting high-level features; - a linear model trained on top of these features can generalize well on a few labeled samples; - the unsupervised learning layers should be adapted to the data at hand; - the best way to adapt the unsupervised layer is to learn the parameters of the unsupervised model from the labeled samples, and use these parameters in the unsupervised phase.

(i) the combination of several one-layer algorithms, with a simple linear classifier, is an effective way to learn a good representation for classification, (ii) the use of deep architectures is not always necessary, and (iii) the combination of different one-layer algorithms is an effective way of using deep architectures.

(1) the best way to learn a deep representation for classification is by stacking several one-layer unsupervi sed learning algorithms, each one adapted to one of the datasets of the competition, and (2) a simple linear classifier can achieve good results when fed with representations learned by the above strategy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1) What are the most effective unsupervised learning strategies for extracting good representations from a given unlabeled set of examples?
the following questions: (1) How to train a deep architecture when only unlabeled data is available?
the following question: how to train deep neural networks with one-layer unsupervized learning algorithms and few labeled samples?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best results were obtained by using a combination of several unsupervised learning methods.
unsupervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning can be very effective in transfer learning.
the best strategy is to combine different one-layer learning algorithms, each adapted to a specific task, and to stack them in a deep architecture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we combined and stacked one layer algorithms, adapted to the data, to learn a good representation, and then we stacked a linear classifier on top of that to learn the final classification.
we used a simple linear classifier, but stacked different kinds of layers on top of it to get better features.

we have shown that a) a simple linear classifier can be trained with very few labeled samples, b) a simple linear classification task can be learned by stacking several one-layer learning algorithms, c) a simple linear model can learn to combine several one-layer learning methods, d) a simple linear combination can be learned from several datasets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is often possible to train a simple classifier on top of a deep learning representation, and achieve state-of-the-art results on the task of interest.
it is possible to combine a large number of different unsupervised learning methods, and that it is also possible to stack them in a way that preserves their respective strengths.
a simple linear model, trained on a good representation, is surprisingly powerful, even when the number of training samples is extremely small.
